title: Intermittent p99 swell after stream-resume: mini-surge window entrapment in continuous batcher
text:
Intermittent p99 swell after stream-resume: mini-surge window entrapment in continuous batcher

description:
Issue summary:
Customer Glyph Analytics started reporting intermittent elevated p99 latencies and occasional request timeouts after a pattern of stream resumes (short streaming sessions resuming after quiet periods). Affected routes are primarily chat streaming endpoints pinned to redwood-mini-1.1 on their dedicated pool.

Impact:
- Frequent p99 increases from baseline ~220ms up to 2.8–3.6s for bursty, short-stream resumes.
- Several customer requests observed as 504 timeouts during sustained resumption waves.
- Impacts production SLAs for Glyph (dedicated contract).

Environment:
- prod us-east-1 (dedicated cluster id: glyph-dedicated-03)
- Runtime: serving-runtime v1.28.3, continuous-batcher v0.9.2
- Traffic pattern: low baseline qps with bursts of 20–120 short streams per second over 30–90s windows

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Idle period of ~5–10 minutes on a subset of client connections.
2) Client resumes streaming sessions in a short burst (many short seqs, avg tokens/request 12–40).
3) Within 15–45s from first resume, p95 stable but p99 climbs non-linearly; some requests hit timeout.

Observed behavior:
- Continuous batcher appears to create a transient cohort (mini-surge window) where many short streams are coalesced but KV cache priming and sequence-length heterogeneity cause repeated micro-batches and head-of-line waiting for longer sequences.

investigation_notes:
Initial hypotheses:
- Cohort entrapment: a small cohort of resumed streams is being repeatedly re-queued into the same micro-batch window causing per-request queuing and repeated kernel invocation overhead.
- Cache warmup contention: resumed streams trigger KV cache misses and synchronous priming paths that block flushes.
- Linger amplification: stream-resume timing aligns with linger timer boundaries creating resonant flushes.

What we've checked so far:
- Confirmed spike correlated with stream-resume waves via Grafana chart 'requests.stream_resume_rate' and 'batcher.flush_latency'.
- Heap/CPU on GPUs not saturated; GPU utilization steady off-peak (40–55%).
- Continuous-batcher logs show repeated small-batch flushes for the affected tenant window between 2026-03-10T14:12:07Z and 2026-03-10T14:13:42Z.
- No config changes on customer side; no recent deployment to serving-runtime in glyph-dedicated-03 during window.
- Timeline aligns with tenant reshuffle event (scheduler shard rebalance) 2026-03-10T14:09Z — possible transient routing change.

Next investigative actions planned:
- Add high-resolution tracing around micro-batch lifecycle and KV priming for tenant glyph on prod cluster.
- Temporarily relax linger threshold and increase max coalesced size for glyph-dedicated-03 to see if p99 drops.
- Correlate per-request KV miss rates with affected request IDs and check for synchronous cache priming code paths.
- Run a canary patch that converts synchronous cache priming to async-prefetch for resumed streams in a single node pool.

Preliminary mitigation (temporary):
- Routed glyph traffic to warm node pool (manual routing override) at 2026-03-11T09:18Z; observed immediate drop in p99 in the next 5 minutes from ~3s to ~420ms for short stream bursts.
- Rolling restart of continuous-batcher worker group on glyph-dedicated-03 reduced repeat micro-batches but did not eliminate p99 spikes during heavy surges.

reproduction_steps:
1) Using a short-stream workload generator (see attached script) open N streams with pause/resume behavior: idle for 300s, then resume 60 streams in 45s window.
2) Send short sequences (10-30 tokens) and enable streaming on the API route pinned to redwood-mini-1.1.
3) Observe Grafana dashboards for 'batcher.flush_latency', 'request.p99', and 'kv_cache.miss_rate'.
4) Repeat with linger threshold lowered by 20ms in config to see effect.

Note: reproduction script run against a lower-traffic dedicated pool reliably provokes the p99 swell when scheduler shard boundaries are exercised.

comments:
Support (Maya Chen) 2026-03-10T15:02: Logged initial report after customer escalated via #support-glyph. Provided request IDs and Grafana link. Requested SRE triage.
SRE (Diego Alvarez) 2026-03-10T16:30: Observed repeated small flushes and KV miss spikes. Hypothesis: sync KV priming in resumed streams causing head-of-line blocking. Will instrument tracing on batch boundaries.
Eng (Liam O'Connor) 2026-03-11T08:45: Started manual routing override to warm pool and performed rolling restarts on batcher workers. Noted p99 reduction immediately; preparing a targeted config tweak (linger + coalesce size) for canary later today.
Customer (Glyph Ops - Priya Reddy) 2026-03-11T09:05: Thank you — saw latency improve after your routing change. Continuing to monitor traffic spikes and will report if timeouts reoccur.
SRE (Diego Alvarez) 2026-03-12T10:12: Added tracing hooks to batcher for tenant cohorts and collected a 2-minute trace capturing repeated requeue events. Uploading trace artifact to artifact store (link in attachments).

resolution:
Mitigation in progress. Temporary routing to warm pool and worker restarts improved p99 but root cause not yet fixed. Next: deploy canary that async-prefetches KV entries for resumed streams and adjust linger/coalesce heuristics. Will update after canary results.

notes_for_followup:
- Validate canary results across multiple dedicated pools and under scheduler shard rebalance.
- Consider a workload-aware 'resume' path that marks streams for async prefetch.
- Add an automated detection alert for cohort entrapment patterns (rapid repeated small flushes with kv miss correlation).
